title: Shape, texture and pattern — Image Wiki
text:
Shape, texture and pattern
  Three of the basic elements every image is made of, and the fact that connects them — they are the same thing seen from three distances.

  
    Termshape, texture, pattern
    Also calledsilhouette, form, surface quality, motif
    Not the same asform as a three-dimensional volume, detail, noise
    Read10 min
  

  
    
      On this page
      
        The three words, kept straightWhy texture is really lightWhat each rung is good forAcross different mediaCommon mistakes
      
    
  

  Stand at the far end of a street and watch someone you know walk towards you. You recognise them long before you can see a face. What you recognised was an outline and the way it moves — a flat patch of dark against the background. Drawabox puts it plainly: the silhouette is the first thing the eye registers, before it considers anything inside it (SRC-078).
Keep watching. At some point their coat stops being a grey patch and becomes tweed — visibly woven, though you cannot see one thread. Closer still and the threads separate into things with edges.
Nothing about the coat changed. You changed distance, and the same physical stuff arrived as a shape, then as a texture, then as a set of shapes again. That is the one idea in this article: shape, texture and pattern are not three different kinds of thing. They are one thing at three viewing distances, and knowing which rung you are on tells you what you can and cannot say about an image.
The three words, kept straight
A shape is a bounded area — height and width, and an outline separating it from its surroundings (SRC-001, SRC-008). Shape is what you see before you recognise the object, and what survives a squint. Getty and the National Gallery both sort shapes into geometric (circles, rectangles, triangles) and organic (the irregular kind you find in a leaf or a puddle) (SRC-001, SRC-014).
Form is the same idea with depth added: a sphere rather than a circle. Smarthistory notes that "form" also gets used for the illusion of three dimensions on a flat surface, which is where the confusion starts (SRC-008). In a photograph everything is literally shape; form is what the shading persuades you of.
Texture is surface variation too fine to read as individual shapes. It tells you what a thing is made of: rough, wet, woven, chalky, greasy. Getty defines it as the property you would sense by touch, delivered to the eye instead (SRC-001).
A pattern is repetition regular enough that you can predict it. Once you can predict it, you stop examining it, and the whole area collapses into a single field. What happens to the gaps in that repetition is a separate subject: Rhythm and repetition.



Katsushika Hokusai, Fine Wind, Clear Morning (Gaifū kaisei), from Thirty-six Views of Mount Fuji, c. 1830–32 (Metropolitan Museum of Art). Public domain.
All three, in one print, kept separate on purpose.
Shape. Fuji is a single flat area of pink-brown with an outline and nothing inside it but a few snow streaks. No modelling, no gradient, no attempt at a volume — and it is instantly a mountain.
Texture. The forest along the lower slope is thousands of small dark marks. Follow it from right to left: near the right they are separated enough that you can pick out an individual tree, and by the left they have merged into an even dark nap where no single mark is findable. That is the shape-to-texture crossing happening inside one band of one picture.
Pattern. The sky is a repeated cloud bar, stacked at regular intervals. You read it once, predict the rest, and stop looking — which is exactly what it is for. The clouds are numerous and high in contrast, and they still do not compete with the mountain.


Why texture is really light
Texture looks like a property of the surface. In an image it is made of shadows.
Drawabox's whole approach rests on this: the lines you perceive as texture are almost all shadows cast by tiny forms sitting on the surface — bumps, pits, scratches, scales, each blocking a little light and dropping a small dark shape beside itself (SRC-078). Texture is a lighting result, not a material fact, and that has two immediate consequences.
Raking light reveals texture; frontal light kills it. Put the source almost parallel to the surface and every bump gets a long shadow; put it behind the camera and the shadows hide behind the bumps that cast them. Same wall, same plaster. See Light direction and Hard and soft light.
Texture density is adjustable without changing the material. Pack the shadow shapes tightly in one area and thin them elsewhere, and the viewer reads more light rather than fewer scales (SRC-078). The dense area becomes a focal point; the sparse one becomes somewhere to rest.



The Palouse hills from Steptoe Butte, Whitman County, Washington. Photograph by Caleb Riston via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY 4.0.
The sun is low and almost sideways, so every hill casts a shadow onto the next one. What you are looking at is not a pattern of dark paint on the ground; it is a field of cast shadows, and it is the reason this landscape has a surface at all.
Then walk your eye from the bottom of the frame to the top. In the foreground each hill is a shape with its own lit face and its own shadow, big enough to hold a farm. Halfway up, the hills are still separable but you have stopped counting them. At the horizon they have become an even fine texture in which no individual hill exists.
One photograph, one hillside type, one light. The rung you are on is decided entirely by how much of the frame each hill occupies.


What each rung is good for

Shapesa roof from two metres awayyou read each tile, and its outlineA patternthe same roof from the pavementregular enough to predict; you stop countingA texturethe same roof from across the valleyno single tile is a shape any more

The same motif in all three panels, arranged the same way. Only its size changes — which means only your distance from the roof changes.
Left, the tiles are shapes: you read each outline, and a chipped one would be an event. Middle, they have become a pattern: still individually visible, regular enough to predict, and you stop inspecting after the first few. Right, they are a texture: the panel now has a material rather than contents, and no single tile is available to look at.
Nothing was redrawn between the panels. If you find yourself arguing about whether something in an image is a shape, a pattern or a texture, the answer is usually "at what size?".


Shape carries recognition and composition, because it survives being small, blurred or squinted at. If the shapes do not read, nothing downstream saves the picture — the same claim Value structure makes about masses, from the other side. Texture carries material, and it is a strong attractor: high-texture areas pull the eye, which is useful over a subject and expensive over a background (SRC-017). Pattern does one of two opposite things, and which one is worth checking every time.



Tilework of the Sheikh Lotfollah Mosque, Isfahan, completed 1619. Photograph by Swissfrog via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY 3.0.
Two patterns, doing opposite jobs, in one frame.
The dome at the lower right is a grid of identical lozenges that shrinks steadily towards the crown. It is completely predictable, so within a second you stop reading tiles and start reading a curved surface — the pattern's job here is to make you see a dome, and it does it by getting smaller.
The blue arabesque on the vaults above is much denser and far less predictable. Look closely and it is a repeated floral unit; look normally and it refuses to resolve, so it reads as a continuous field with no findable subject. It swallows anything placed on it, which is precisely why the band of white calligraphy running between the vaults sits on a plain dark ground instead. Change nothing about the writing and put it on the arabesque, and it disappears.





Attic black-figure neck-amphora, near the Medea Group, c. 510 BCE (J. Paul Getty Museum, CC0 via the Getty Open Content Program).
The same three rungs, this time on one pot, and useful because the shapes are literally flat.
Shape. Achilles and Ajax are solid black silhouettes. There is no shading and no volume, and you still read two armoured men leaning in over a board, plus Athena standing between them — because the outlines were designed to be legible. Notice what the painter did with the helmet crests and the spear shafts: they break the silhouette, so they read instantly.
Texture. Look inside the black. The scale armour, the shield rims and the hair are fine incised lines scratched through the slip. Individually they are invisible from a metre away; together they say metal, wool, hair.
Pattern. Three bands — palmettes at the neck, a meander below the figures, petals at the foot — each regular enough that you check a couple of units and accept the rest. They frame without competing, which is what patterns are for on an object whose subject is in the middle.


Across different media

Drawing and painting. Texture is implied. Drawabox insists on drawing the cast shadow shapes rather than outlining each textural form, because outlining everything produces noise the eye cannot leave (SRC-078).
Photography. You cannot add texture, only light it. Time of day is the control.
3D. The three rungs are separate channels — silhouette from geometry, texture from a roughness or normal map, pattern from a tiled image — and a render most often looks wrong because a pattern was tiled at the wrong scale for the camera distance.

Common mistakes

"Shape means the outline someone drew." An area of flat colour with no line around it is a shape too. Anything your eye can separate from its surroundings has one.
"Texture is detail." Detail is information you can read; texture is variation too fine to resolve into parts. Megapixels do not convert one into the other — moving closer does.
"Smooth means no texture." Smooth is a texture, read from the specular highlight instead of from shadows. See Diffuse and specular.
"Pattern is decoration." It turns many objects into one field. That is structural, and it can hide your subject as easily as unify your frame.
"They are three different properties." They are three readings of the same marks, chosen by scale. Settle the viewing distance before arguing about the label.


Sorting an image into the three

Squint hard. What is left are the shapes. Name three of them.
Check the subject against the background as a silhouette. Is its outline still separable, or does it merge? If it merges, see Gestalt grouping.
Find the largest area of texture. Where is its light coming from — and is it over the subject or over the background?
Find any pattern. Decide whether it is unifying the frame or hiding something in it.
Ask what would happen at half the viewing distance. Textures would become shapes, and some patterns would stop being predictable — that is the same picture on a different rung.



  
    
      Read next
      
        
          
            
              Light direction
              Where the light sits relative to the subject and to the camera. It decides where the shadows land and how much of the shaded side you get to see, which is what makes a flat picture look solid.
            
          
        
          
            
              Value structure
              How light or dark things are, independent of their colour. Squint at any image and what survives is its value structure — and if that does not read, no colour will save it.
            
          
        
          
            
              Gestalt grouping
              The automatic machinery that turns a field of pixels into objects and groups — and the reason accidental alignments in a photograph look deliberate.
            
          
        
          
            
              Rhythm and repetition
              Repeating something turns many things into one thing — and the moment it does, whatever does not belong to the set becomes impossible to miss.
